Part 01 · Overview

Keep a sale and an operating plan both ready, and choose on 22 January.

Comvest should not approve the company's request of 19 October. It should offer one standstill to 31 March 2027: a written promise not to enforce the loan, in return for a budget, new money that is repaid first, and dated steps toward a sale. By 22 January the lenders will know what a buyer would pay and whether an operating plan has passed an independent test. They sell if the best offer is close to what owning the business would return, and take ownership if it is clearly lower.

Two minutesThe summary and the plan on one pageTen minutesThe rest of this tabThe detailParts 02 to 08WordsPoint at a dotted term for its meaning, or see the list of terms

Do now

Reserve rights, check the cash at the bank, and offer the standstill by 4 December. None of it needs new money.

Decide on 22 January

Sell, take ownership and collect the cash, or take ownership and run an operating plan. One rule, fixed in advance, picks the path.

What it is worth

About $6.7M to Comvest from a sale. About $7.4M to $11.3M from operating if search revenue holds, and about $2.8M if it keeps falling.

The route is clear, four findings need watching, and nothing is yet checked.

A single route runs to decision day, and three paths follow it.

The work to 22 January is the same whatever happens next: a standstill, a sale process run by a banker, and an operating plan tested by people who did not write it. On decision day the lenders choose between a sale, owning and collecting, and owning and operating. A run-off and a sale of the loan stay available behind them.

The three paths differ in who owns Sleep Media, and for how long. A sale ends the lenders' involvement in March. Ownership keeps it for up to two years and needs more new money first.

Part 02 · Situation · What do the records show?

Sleep Media earns the money, Sleep Care spends it, and the loan's deadlines are close.

Sleep Media earns about $13M before shared cost, and Sleep Care and head office spend about $17M. Google sends about half the clicks of a year ago, and revenue has held because more of them go on to a seller at a higher price. Three loan tests fall before 31 March.

Read the detail · 02 Situation

Part 03 · Value · What is a sale worth?

A sale returns about $6.7M to Comvest, and signed partner terms matter most.

The base case is 11 cents per dollar of Comvest's loan, and the four sale cases run from $4.8M to $15.1M. Signed 2027 partner terms are the largest single step up. Whether owning beats selling depends on what happens to earnings.

Read the detail · 03 Value

Part 04 · Funding · What does it cost to get there?

Each path needs some new money first, and three levers shrink it.

Cash falls by about $3.6M between 30 November and 31 March, so holding $2.0M needs about $2.8M. A partner paying in advance, a domain sale and a new owner for Sleep Care bring that to about $0.4M. Ownership uses about $2M more than a sale.

Read the detail · 04 Funding

Part 05 · Route · How is the choice made?

A single process leads to decision day, and then to a sale or to ownership.

One standstill to 31 March carries a budget, the new money and the sale dates. On 22 January the lenders sell unless ownership beats the best offer by a clear margin. A fair offer of about $15M about matches ownership if search holds and nothing more, and falls short of it if the plan lands.

Read the detail · 05 Route

Part 06 · Operate · What if the lenders own and run it?

Owning and running Sleep Media pays more than a sale if search revenue holds.

Ownership returns about $7.4M to Comvest if search holds and $11.3M if the cost and revenue plan lands, against $6.7M from a sale. It returns about $2.8M if search keeps falling. The break-even is a fall in search of about 2% a year, and five stop rules limit the loss.

Read the detail · 06 Operate

Part 07 · Businesses · What happens to each business?

Keep Sleep Media steady, cap Sleep Care, and settle its future in January.

Nothing a reader or Google sees changes before decision day. Sleep Care's paid marketing is capped, and a new owner by 31 January is worth $2.3M to Comvest against none. Sleep Foundation leads its field on search visits.

Read the detail · 07 Businesses

Part 08 · Execution · Who does what, and when?

Most first steps start this week, and the largest risks are read by year end.

Fourteen of twenty first steps start before Thanksgiving and need nothing signed by the borrower. The largest risks are the level of click-outs after Google's update and the partner terms, and both are known by 31 December.

Read the detail · 08 Execution

Eighteen decisions are asked of Comvest, most of them before signing.

Each line links to the section that supports it. The standstill is signed on 11 December, and fifteen of the eighteen fall on or before that date. Arrangements for advisers and managers are approved separately, by people independent of the party concerned, and nothing in the plan depends on them.

Part 02 · The business, the loan and Google

Sleep Media earns the money, Sleep Care spends it, and the loan's deadlines are close.

This part sets out what the company's own records show: the two businesses, the loan and its dates, and the Google traffic that Sleep Media lives on. Actual figures run to August 2026, and later months are management's forecast.

The business

Sleep Media earned about $8.7M on its own in the year to August. Sleep Care and head office spent more than that.

The loan

About $190M of debt sits on a business worth $11M to $30M, so the senior lenders are the owners in all but name.

The clock

Interest starts to fall due in cash after 30 November, and three loan tests come before 31 March.

Sleep Media earns the money, and Sleep Care and head office spend more.

OneCare Media trades as Sleep Doctor and runs two businesses inside one borrower. Sleep Media publishes sleepfoundation.org and earns a commission when a reader clicks through to a seller. Sleep Care sells home sleep apnea tests and CPAP breathing machines, for cash and since 2026 through insurance.

What holds. Sleep Media earns about $13M before shared costs on management's forecast, which is enough to carry a much smaller loan.

What to watch. Sleep Care and head office together spend about $17M, so the company as a whole loses money.

Sources: long-range plan of 21 October 2026.

Sleep Media is profitable and shrinking, and the forecast needs a strong finish.

Sleep Media earned about $8.7M standing on its own over the twelve months to August 2026, on $14.4M of revenue. Revenue fell 18% in the first eight months of 2026 against the same months a year earlier.

What holds. The earnings are real and recent: the twelve months to August are all actual figures.

What to watch. Management's forecast needs September to December revenue to run 41% above a year earlier, after eight months that ran below.

Sleep Care's loss has grown as it has sold more.

Sleep Care fulfilled about 2.4 times as many sleep studies a month in August 2026 as in 2024, and its monthly loss about doubled. Management's plan for 2027 needs revenue to rise 2.7 times and still shows a loss.

What holds. The business has a working way to win patients, contracts with insurers and a repeat-order book that earns about $1.0M a year.

What to watch. Its break-even date has been moved three times and now stands at October 2027.

Sources: monthly reporting packages; long-range plan.

The debt is many times what the business is worth.

The senior loan was $100.6M in September 2026 and reaches $103.1M in December as unpaid interest is added to it. Another lender, Falcon, holds $85.9M of junior notes that rank behind it. On each case in this document, the value reaches the senior loan and nothing below it.

What holds. The senior lenders are the only parties with money still at stake, which gives them the standing to set terms.

What to watch. Comvest's 58.9% share is from an April 2024 list, and the current list of lenders has not been seen.

Three loan tests fall before the end of March, and the forecast passes none.

Until 30 November 2026 interest is added to the loan in place of being paid. After that it falls due in cash, at about $0.9M a month. A test that the company holds $2.0M of cash runs monthly to 28 February 2027, and a test of $2.0M of earnings falls on 31 March 2027.

What holds. The company cannot pass these tests on its own forecast, so it needs the lenders' patience, and patience can carry conditions.

What to watch. The date of the first cash interest payment sits in loan documents that have not been seen.

Google sends fewer readers, and a higher price per click has held revenue.

Google clicks on sleepfoundation.org were 975K in October 2026 against 1,874K a year earlier. Revenue fell far less, because a larger share of readers clicked through to a seller, and each click-out earned more under the largest partner's guaranteed price.

What holds. Clicks on the pages that earn the money held up through the first week of Google's November update.

What to watch. Both supports are measured to August 2026 and no later, and the guaranteed price expires on 31 December.

A larger share of clicks now goes on to a seller. The share rose from about 11% in the second half of 2025 to about 16% in June to August 2026. That is why click-outs held near 40K to 45K a week while Google clicks fell.

Part 03 · What a sale is worth

A sale returns about $6.7M to Comvest, and signed partner terms matter most.

This part builds the value of Sleep Media step by step, from weekly clicks to Comvest's share. It sets out four cases and a severe one, and tests each input. Each case here is a sale that closes on 31 March 2027. Part 06 values the alternative, which is to own and run the business.

How value is built

Weekly clicks to sellers, times what each earns, less running cost, times the years of earnings a buyer pays.

The cases

Four cases turn on two facts known by 31 December: are partner terms signed, and do click-outs hold?

Sell or own

A sale wins if earnings keep falling. Ownership shows more if they hold. The sale cases assume they fall.

The base case returns about $6.7M to Comvest on the evidence available today.

Search revenue is weekly click-outs times 52 times revenue per click-out. Other revenue is added and the cost of running Sleep Media on its own is taken off. A buyer pays a number of years of those earnings. Selling cost and the costs the old company leaves behind come off the price, and the result is put in today's money.

What holds. The model was built from two separate analyses of the same records, and it reproduces each of their values before any input is changed.

What to watch. No input rests on a bank statement, a signed loan document, a supplier's quote or an offer.

Signed partner terms move Comvest's value more than click-out volume does.

Two questions pick the case. Are 2027 partner terms signed, in a form that carries over to a new owner, by 31 December? Do weekly click-outs hold at 27,000 or more after Google's update? No blended value is shown, because both answers arrive by 31 December.

What holds. Signed terms with lower click-outs return more to Comvest than unsigned terms with click-outs holding.

What to watch. A fall below 21,000 click-outs a week for two weeks is the severe case, in which a sale has no value to the lenders.

A signed price floor is the first step to the best case. On its own it adds about $3.1M for Comvest. The rest of the gain needs volume, other revenue and the higher price a buyer pays for contracted revenue.

Private · what this means for you

On the proposed terms these four cases pay you $0.37M, $0.47M, $0.74M and $1.59M in total, from the weakest to the best, for about four months' work.

Click-outs and revenue per click-out move the base case more than any other input.

Each test changes one input on the base case and holds the rest. The two revenue inputs come first, and the price a buyer pays follows. Cost matters most where a buyer pays for a saving it can see.

What holds. Each of the largest gains is something the plan works on directly: partner terms, a new owner for Sleep Care, the bid form and a quoted budget.

What to watch. The gains do not simply add up, because click-outs and revenue per click-out multiply.

Whether to sell or to own turns on what happens to earnings.

If the lenders take ownership and search revenue keeps falling by 15% a year, a later sale returns less than a sale in March. If search revenue holds, ownership returns more. The sale cases assume the fall, because nothing in the record yet shows otherwise.

What holds. A sale is cash in March, and it does not depend on what Google does next.

What to watch. A buyer who pays three years of earnings is paid to carry the risk of decline, and keeps that reward if earnings hold.

Owning without a plan to change the trend loses in each case. If the lenders take ownership, keep today's team and collect cash while search falls, a later buyer is assumed to pay 2.5 times earnings for a smaller business. Part 06 sets out the plan that would change the trend.

Private · what this means for you

If the lenders operate and choose you, the role would pay you more in total than a sale: about $0.9M to $1.6M over 28 months, against $0.47M over four. Say so before Comvest works it out.

The sale case is about half the value lenders showed in September.

Lenders carried the loan in their accounts at 22.5 cents per dollar on 30 September 2026, which implies $13.7M for Comvest. A sale at 3.0 times earnings reaches that value with next-year earnings of about $9.2M. A value in a lender's accounts is the lender's own estimate, and no buyer has put a price on it.

What holds. The case with signed terms and click-outs holding clears that value.

What to watch. An indicative offer for Comvest's loan is the market test, and asking for one is among the decisions.

Part 04 · Cash and new money

Each path needs some new money first, and three levers shrink it.

This part follows the cash from 30 November to 31 March, the cost of the changes, the levers that reduce the need, the terms proposed for the new money and the stress tests. It also shows what ownership would need beyond a sale.

To March

Holding $2.0M of cash to 31 March needs about $2.8M of new money, or about $0.4M if three levers land.

If the lenders own

About $3.8M in total, about $2M more than a sale uses. The business pays it back from its own cash.

Why fund at all

The lenders already fund the company through unpaid interest, with no say over how it is spent.

Cash falls below the floor in December and below zero by March.

The cash path runs from 30 November 2026 to a closing on 31 March 2027. Receipts are the collection of earlier months' revenue on the company's own schedule. Payments are the cost of running Sleep Media and five lines of one-off cost.

What holds. No cash interest is paid on this path and the domain proceeds stay in the business, and the standstill has to put both in writing.

What to watch. Opening cash is the company's forecast and not a bank balance, and $1.9M of it is domain-sale proceeds.

What holds. A cap on paid marketing lowers Sleep Care's monthly cash use while its patients, contracts and staff stay in place.

What to watch. No line has been quoted, and the range across the Sleep Care outcomes is $4.9M to $7.4M.

Ownership uses about $2M more than a sale, and for longer.

In a sale, the price pays the selling cost and the costs the old company leaves behind. If the lenders take ownership there is no price, so they fund those costs, the cost of the transfer and the first weeks of the new company. That comes to about $3.8M before the levers, against the $2.8M needed to reach March.

What holds. The new company earns about $0.4M a month, so it is out of the red within three months and repays the lenders from its own cash.

What to watch. Comvest has said it will put in no new money, and its share here would be about $2.2M before the levers.

Part 05 · The route and decision day

A single process leads to decision day, and then to a sale or to ownership.

This part shows the route step by step. Use the explorer below to see which path the rule picks under different readings, offers and beliefs. Nothing here is legal advice, and each step that depends on the loan documents is marked for counsel.

To 22 January

One standstill, one sale process and one tested operating plan, run side by side.

On decision day

Sell, unless ownership on a tested plan beats the best offer by a clear margin.

The open question

A fair offer about matches ownership if search holds and nothing more. Ownership wins if the plan lands, or if offers come in low.

The path depends on the readings, the offers and the tested plan.

Three things are known by the middle of January: what the December readings show, the best offer for Sleep Media, and whether the operating plan has passed its test. Choose an answer to each, and the explorer shows the path the rule picks, what it is worth to Comvest and what happens next.

What holds. The rule is fixed before the offers arrive, so the choice on the day follows the evidence and not the mood.

What to watch. On today's working case a fair offer about matches ownership if search holds and nothing more, so that close call goes to the cash.

The whole rule fits on one grid. On today's working case, each square shows the path for one offer and one reading of the plan. The outlined square is the choice made in the explorer.

A standstill and a single transfer keep each path open to March.

The lenders agree a standstill: a written promise not to enforce the loan until 31 March, in return for a budget, dates and tests. The company's board, an independent officer and one banker run the sale. Sleep Media then changes hands once, on 31 March, to a buyer or to the lenders.

What holds. A single transfer means partners and suppliers are asked to consent once, and the lenders see a market price before they decide.

What to watch. Taking the company first would make the lenders the owner of a healthcare business before any offer is seen.

An offer has to beat what the lenders can show ownership would return.

The minimum price is the offer below which the lenders do better by owning, after a margin for the risk. If ownership means collecting cash from a shrinking business, it is about $9M. If a tested plan shows search revenue holding, it is about $15M, and about $18M with the team down to six. A fair offer is about $15M.

What holds. Ownership has to beat an offer by the greater of $1.0M and 10%, so a close call goes to the cash offer.

What to watch. The operating plan comes from CreditSwan's own review, so the independent officer and the banker test it, and CreditSwan does not.

Decision day has five outcomes. Each has a test that can be read on the day. Where an offer and ownership are close, or a condition for ownership is not met, the lenders sell.

Private · what this means for you

The operating plan is your own review. The rule asks the officer and the banker to test it and gives a close call to the cash offer. Do not press the point yourself.

Part 06 · Operate and grow: the third path

Owning and running Sleep Media pays more than a sale if search revenue holds.

On this path the lenders take ownership of Sleep Media on 31 March 2027, appoint an operator and a small team, and sell within about two years. The legal step is the same as owning and collecting cash. What differs is the plan: protect what earns the money, lower cost by stages, add revenue, and stop early if search keeps falling.

What you need to believe

That search revenue can be held about flat. The break-even is a fall of about 2% a year.

What it pays

About $7.4M to Comvest if search holds and $11.3M if the plan lands, against $6.7M from a sale.

What it risks

About $2.8M if search keeps falling to 2029. Stopping at the first review holds the loss to about $1.6M to $2.6M.

The lenders take ownership, appoint an operator and sell within two years.

Three paths follow decision day. A sale ends the lenders' involvement in March. Owning and collecting keeps today's team and takes the cash while the business shrinks. Operating and growing adds an accountable operator and a plan, and gives the business up to two years to show steadier earnings before it is sold.

What holds. The first 60 days are the same on each path, so nothing is given up by keeping the third one open.

What to watch. The loan falls due on 31 December 2027, nine months after a takeover, and counsel has to confirm how a lender-owned company deals with that date.

Ownership would last up to two years. The first review falls six months after the takeover and the second a year after. The sale window opens in mid-2028 and closes in March 2029.

The business repays the new money from its own cash before any sale.

If search holds, the lenders have their new money back by November 2028, and the later sale comes on top.

What holds. The new money is repaid first, ahead of the existing loan, on any outcome where the business earns.

What to watch. If search falls fast the pay-outs do not cover the new money before a sale, which is why the stop rules are read every quarter.

Sleep Care can stay open at a small size if it covers its own cost.

Sleep Care loses about $8M a year, and its own records show where. Winning new patients through paid marketing loses about $1M a year after its costs. Repeat orders from existing patients earn about $1M a year. The loss is the $8M of overhead built to grow. A unit of about six people serving existing patients would about break even, and it would keep something to sell.

What holds. Kept small, it costs about the same as winding it down, so a later sale would be upside: each $1M of price is worth about $0.4M to Comvest.

What to watch. A larger unit that also serves unpaid demand loses about $0.5M a year on these figures, and no team list or quote yet supports either design.

The small design about covers its cost, and the larger one does not. The estimate uses the profit that repeat sales earned in 2026 and a cost for six or twelve people. A 60-day test would replace the estimate with a result.

Sleep Care has three possible futures. A new owner by 31 January is still the best of them. Keeping a small unit is the alternative to a funded wind-down if no new owner signs.

Five stop rules end the path before losses build.

The path is a bet that search revenue can be held. Each rule names a reading that shows the bet is going wrong and what happens next. The business is kept ready for sale throughout, so stopping takes weeks and not months.

What holds. If search keeps falling and the lenders stop at the first review, Comvest gets back about $4.1M to $5.2M, against $2.8M by carrying on.

What to watch. Trying and stopping still costs about $1.6M to $2.6M against a sale in March, and about $3.5M if the fall is fast.

Stopping early is worth $1M or more if search is falling. The gap widens the faster search falls, because each further quarter is spent owning a smaller business.

The lenders choose the operator, and a board of three holds the controls.

Six conditions are met before the lenders choose this path. The plan is tested by people independent of its author. The lenders name the operator. Partners confirm they will carry on. The money is committed, counsel is content and the reading on search is clean.

What holds. The operator answers to a board with two people named by the lenders and one independent, and never approves a contract with a business of their own.

What to watch. CreditSwan wrote the plan and its principal could be a candidate to operate it, so the choice of operator is made without CreditSwan in the room.

Four roles divide the decisions. The lenders set the rules and the money. The board approves the budget and the reviews. The operator runs the plan, and the general manager runs the site.

You could be a candidate for operator. The plan says the choice is made without you in the room, and that is the right answer to the conflict.

Sleep Media

Nothing a reader or Google sees changes before decision day. The work goes into partner terms.

Sleep Care

Paid marketing is capped now. A new owner is sought by 31 January, with a small unit as the alternative to a wind-down.

After decision day the work follows the calendar of the path chosen.

A sale closes about ten weeks after decision day and the work ends by the summer. Owning and collecting runs to a sale by mid-2028. Operating and growing runs to a sale by March 2029, with a review every six months.

What holds. Each calendar starts from the same takeover or closing date of 31 March 2027.

What to watch. Both ownership calendars run past the date the loan falls due, which counsel has to settle before decision day.

The three largest risks can each be read before the year ends.

The largest risk is that Google's update cuts the pages that earn the money. The second is that the partner's guaranteed price lapses with nothing in its place. The third is that click-outs settle at the lower level. Each is known by 31 December, three weeks before decision day.

What holds. A signed price more than makes up for lower click-outs.

What to watch. Risks arrive together: a fall in click-outs in December would also weaken the partner talks and the offers. Under ownership, the same risk continues after March.

The document sets out a plan, and it checks nothing at source.

Method · what this document does

It sets out one route for the senior lenders to decision day and the three paths that follow, with what each is worth, what each costs, the dates and the open items.

Method · what it does not do

It checks nothing against source systems, and it gives no legal, tax or healthcare regulatory advice. It does not set the value Comvest carries in its accounts or the return it requires.

Method · how a sale is valued

Weekly click-outs times 52 times revenue per click-out, plus other revenue, less the cost of running Sleep Media on its own, give earnings for the twelve months from closing. A buyer pays a number of years of those earnings. Selling cost and leftover costs come off, the result is put in today's money at 15% a year, and Comvest takes its 58.9% share.

Method · how ownership is valued

Month by month from April 2027, the new company's earnings build its cash. Cash above $2.0M is paid to the lenders each month. The business is then sold at a stated number of years of the next twelve months' earnings. Each amount is put in today's money at 15% a year.

Method · how the cases are set

Two readings select the sale case: whether 2027 partner terms are signed, and whether click-outs hold at 27,000 a week or more. No odds and no blended value are shown.

Caution · where the models come from

The sale model was built from two separate analyses of the same records. The ownership model was built for this document and matched to the sale model's values for owning and collecting, with three inputs set to make them agree. Neither has had an outside review.

Caution · the author and the operating plan

CreditSwan wrote the operating plan, and its principal could be a candidate to carry it out. The plan therefore asks the independent officer and the banker to test it, and the lenders to choose the operator without CreditSwan in the room.

Sources

Company update of 19 October 2026; long-range plan of 21 October 2026; cash forecasts of 2 and 30 October 2026; Search Console exports of 4 and 16 November 2026; Sleep Care dashboard of 15 November 2026; public filings and rules named in each exhibit.

Twenty-five terms are used with a fixed meaning.

The document uses a plain name for each idea and keeps to it. The label on each card is the word a lender or a lawyer would use for the same thing. In the text, a dotted line under a term opens its meaning.

Part 10 · Frequently asked questions

Most questions turn on evidence that arrives by the middle of January.

Twenty-three questions a lender would ask about this plan, each with the short answer first. Each answer points to the exhibit that carries the figures.

Scope

It is a plan for the senior lenders, built from the company's own records and from public sources.

It sets out what to do in the next ten days, the route to decision day on 22 January, the three paths that follow, what each costs and what each is worth. It is not a diligence pack: it checks nothing against source systems, and it gives no legal, tax or healthcare regulatory advice. Exhibit 8.23 lists what has to be checked first.

Actual figures run to August 2026.

Later months of 2026 and each later year are management's forecast or a case in the models. Values are in today's money, which means discounted at 15% a year to 19 November 2026. Exhibit 3.17 shows the build of a sale line by line.

Eighteen decisions, most of them before the standstill is signed on 11 December.

The first three need no new money and fall due by 25 November. Exhibit 8.14 lists each decision with its date, and the Decisions section of the Overview links each one to its evidence.

Interpretation

The record does not support odds.

Two readings pick the sale case, and both arrive by 31 December: whether 2027 partner terms are signed, and whether click-outs hold after Google's update. The document shows the four cases and the severe case in Exhibit 3.02, and the evidence that selects between them.

That value implies earnings well above what the record supports today.

The base case values a business with Google clicks about a quarter below the summer level and no signed successor to the partner's guaranteed price. Exhibit 3.07 shows the earnings a sale would need, and Exhibit 2.14 sets those values beside the cases.

Sellers pay for click-outs, so they are the unit that earns revenue.

Google clicks fell by about half in a year while click-outs held, because a rising share of clicks went on to a seller, as Exhibit 2.08 shows. Google clicks are kept as an early warning.

The legal step is the same, and the plan is different.

Collecting keeps today's team and takes the cash while the business shrinks. Operating adds an accountable operator, a staged cost plan, a revenue plan and stop rules. Exhibit 6.01 sets the three paths side by side.

Each opens on a stated case and shows Comvest's value against a floor.

Each driver has evidence behind its range. Exhibit 3.08 covers a sale and opens on the base case. Exhibit 6.06 covers ownership and opens on search holding.

Provenance

Company figures come from the long-range plan, the update to lenders of 19 October, the monthly packages, the cash forecasts and the Search Console exports.

Sale values come from the recovery model, which was built from two separate analyses of the same records. Ownership values come from a month-by-month model built for this document. Each exhibit names its source in its closing line.

The signed loan documents, a bank statement and the current list of lenders have not been seen.

Weekly click-outs were last matched for August 2026. No line of cost is quoted, and no offer exists for either business. Exhibit 8.06 shows the coverage by business function.

It reproduces the sale model's values for owning and collecting to within $0.1M on the base case, as Exhibit 6.38 shows.

Three of its inputs were set to make that match, and the register lists them. The figures for operating and growing are new and have had no outside review, so the plan asks the independent officer and the banker to test them.

The largest is the level of weekly click-outs.

Each 5K click-outs a week moves Comvest by about $2.4M in a sale, as Exhibit 3.04 shows. Below about 21,000 a week for two weeks the severe case applies, and any offer is then compared with a run-off, as Exhibit 3.13 sets out.

Findings

Not without help.

Cash crosses the $2.0M floor in December on the base case, as Exhibit 4.01 shows. The plan asks for a commitment of up to $3.0M of repaid-first money, and three levers can bring the amount used down to about $0.4M, as Exhibit 4.03 shows. Ownership needs more, as Exhibit 4.05 shows.

It depends on what happens to earnings.

A sale returns more if search revenue keeps falling, and ownership returns more if it holds, as Exhibit 3.05 shows. The plan keeps both ready and chooses on 22 January, when the readings, the offers and the tested plan are in hand.

Search revenue would have to fall by less than about 2% a year on today's team, as Exhibit 6.05 shows.

With the team down to six the break-even is a fall of about 9% a year. Exhibit 6.03 shows the value in each outcome.

Five stop rules, read every quarter, as Exhibit 6.14 sets out.

If search keeps falling and the lenders stop at the first review, Comvest gets back about $4.1M to $5.2M, as Exhibit 6.15 shows. That is still less than a sale in March.

Separation removes most of the cost and AI a smaller part, as Exhibit 7.02 shows.

About six to nine people's work remains in testing, review, partners and judgement, as Exhibit 7.03 shows. A single employee costs about the same as a core team of six and rests the business on one person.

They are served on each route.

Tests in progress, paid orders, therapy support, claims and records are funded before any pay-out to the lenders, and each duty has a named owner. Exhibit 7.27 sets out the cap, and Exhibit 7.30 sets out how each route treats the Medicare enrolment.

At a small size, about.

Its loss is overhead, and its repeat business makes money, as Exhibit 6.11 shows. A unit of about six people serving existing patients would about break even, as Exhibit 6.12 shows. No team list or quote supports that yet, so a 60-day test comes first.

Process

Counsel reads the signed loan documents, rights are reserved, an information wall goes around the Saatva credit, and the company supplies bank statements and confirms the domain renewal.

None of it needs anything signed by the borrower. Exhibit 8.16 lists the first five working days.

Lenders holding a majority of the loan decide, on a paper from the board's independent officer and the banker, against a rule adopted before offers arrive.

Exhibit 5.05 lists the outcomes and the test for each, and Exhibit 5.04 shows the minimum price by what ownership would do.

An operator chosen by the lenders, above today's general manager, answering to a board of three.

Exhibit 6.17 sets out who decides what. CreditSwan wrote the operating plan, so the choice is made without CreditSwan in the room.

Yes.

Nothing in it depends on any adviser or management arrangement, and those are approved separately by people independent of the party concerned. The lenders' adviser supports three workstreams and owns none, as Exhibit 8.19 shows.

Private

Between $0.37M and $1.59M in total, for about four months.

Because the hurdle decides whether the base case pays an award at all.

Part 11 · Private · The mandate proposal

The proposed mandate pays for time, for a closing and for recovery above a hurdle.

This tab sets out the operating mandate that the lenders' adviser would ask Comvest to approve, separately from the plan. It covers the terms, what they cost the lenders in each case, the work, the safeguards and the terms if the lenders take ownership and choose the adviser to run Sleep Media. No term has been agreed, and nothing in the plan depends on it.

Private until sent

This tab is the request you would send to Comvest as its own document, after the plan. It holds Part X and nothing from your private notes. It is left out of an edition built for sharing unless you choose to include it.

The retainer pays for time, and the award pays above the lenders' walk-away value.

The proposal has three parts. A retainer of $30K a month runs from 1 December to closing. A completion fee of $250K is earned on a sale, a transfer to the lenders or a sale of Comvest's loan. An award of 7.5% applies to lender cash above a hurdle, and the fee is credited against it.

What holds. The hurdle is the value of the best alternative open to the lenders at signing, and Comvest fixes it without the adviser. The proposed reference is a forced sale, $7.0M for the four lenders today.

What to watch. Securities and tax counsel have to confirm the structure of the fee and the award before signing. If a firm bid for the loan implies a higher walk-away value, that figure is the hurdle.

A later closing lowers the award, and Comvest controls any longer retainer.

What to watch. In the two weakest cases the fee is flat, so each month that Comvest extends adds one month of retainer.

The plan and the mandate are separate decisions.

The adviser wrote the plan and attends the company's board for the lenders without a vote. An author who would be paid under the plan has a conflict. It is handled by keeping the two decisions apart: Comvest judges the plan on its evidence, and approves or declines the mandate separately.

What holds. The plan leans to a sale that would end the engagement in about four months, and ownership pays where it beats the bid that was turned down.

What to watch. The urgent steps do not wait for this decision. The reservation of rights, counsel, verified cash and the standstill go ahead whatever is decided.

Sources: board observer term sheet of 28 January 2025; Part X of the private master.

If the lenders operate, the role becomes a chair at their option.

The operating path needs an operator, and the lenders choose one. If they choose the adviser, the engagement converts to an executive-chair agreement at MediaCo, above the general manager. The chair fee is $25K a month for six months and $20K after, with the same 7.5% award above a hurdle that is reset once on decision day. The lenders are free to appoint someone else, and the completion fee is then the adviser's last payment.

What holds. The reset hurdle is the best offer turned down plus the margin for risk, so an award is paid where operating beats the sale that was declined. If a fair offer is declined, the hurdle is about $12.7M for the four lenders.

What to watch. Over about 28 months the role pays about twice a March sale before any award. The adviser wrote the operating plan, so the plan asks others to test it and the lenders to choose the operator without the adviser in the room.

Five terms govern the chair role. The lenders decide who operates. The role sits above a general manager and has no part in Sleep Care.

The next three weeks decide whether you are engaged, and on what terms.

This tab is written to you. It lists what to do this week, the order in which to send things, how to make sure you are paid, what to ask your own lawyer and what to avoid. The engagement would be signed with the standstill on 11 December.

Private · you only

Not for Comvest, the company or any other party. This tab is left out of any edition built for sharing.

Five items protect your position before any of this is agreed.

Your term sheet caps you at $5,000 a quarter without written consent, it is unsigned, and its indemnity covers attendance as an observer. The work under way since 3 November is already beyond it.

What holds. The interim consent is an easy yes, it is owed, and it resets the anchor for the retainer.

What to watch. The insurance policy on file ran to 29 September 2026 and no renewal is in the folder. If it was not renewed, an election may fall due on 28 November.

Sources: board observer term sheet of 28 January 2025; correspondence of December 2025 and April 2026; the insurance policy on file.

Send the plan first, and the request before the budget is fixed.

The plan goes first and carries no part of your request. The request follows by 24 November as its own short document. The term sheet goes to the borrower with a budget on 4 December, and that is the natural date for an answer.

What holds. Sending the plan first lets Comvest judge it on its evidence, which is the first safeguard in the request.

What to watch. Do not hold a time-critical lender protection behind your own negotiation. Say plainly that the protections should proceed whatever the answer is.

Sources: Part Y of the private master; CreditSwan timetable.

A fee that is not in the funds flow is an unsecured claim.

The company has about $190M of debt against a business worth about $15M on the base case. A fee owed by the company and left outside the closing funds flow would rank behind that debt.

What holds. Written into the agent's order of payments at closing as a lender expense, the fee and the award are paid after the repaid-first funding and before the in proportion distribution.

What to watch. Who can approve and pay each element is a question for your own counsel, and it is the third of the twelve.

Draft note · to send in your own words

The attached replaces the 17 November plan. I had the plan tested twice, independently, and rebuilt in one model. Four things changed. Value from a sale is lower: about $6.7M for Comvest on the base case against $14.9M, because it no longer counts cash at closing, a partner price that is unsigned or a sale price that no offer supports. The path needs funding: up to $3.0M of new money that is repaid first, which three levers can cut to about $0.4M. Sleep Media changes hands once, on a decision day of 22 January, not twice. And the plan now sets out what owning and operating Sleep Media would return, with the test it has to pass first: it beats a sale if search revenue holds, and it loses if search keeps falling. The first steps are unchanged and should start this week. I would rather you had the lower number from me now than from a banker in January.

Comvest as a CreditSwan customer is worth more than the award.

What to watch. Bring no proposal for tooling at MediaCo or at a buyer until the mandate is settled.

The questions cover your capacity on each date, the terms that bind today, who can approve and pay, how the fee and award are documented, insurance, licensing, tax and what survives termination.

What to watch. None of the twelve has been put to counsel.

The sale values are unchanged, and the third path sits beside them.

Version 5.1 keeps the route, the cases and the sale values of 5.0. It adds the operate-and-grow path with its own model, a way to keep Sleep Care open at a small size, a rule for decision day that gives a close call to the cash offer, and a rewrite in plain words. The edition for sharing carries no version wording.

What holds. The rebuilt ownership model matches the published ownership values to within $0.1M on the base case, and the simulator in the page agrees with the model.

What to watch. The minimum price is defined differently from 5.0, and the figures for operating are new. Neither has had an outside review.

Three plans were read in full, and each was right about something different.

The 17 November plan had the fullest statement of the lenders' rights, the separation and the operating model. The independent plan had the evidence standard and the underwriting. The 19 November rebuild had the funded route and one transfer on a single decision day.

What holds. Where two sources agree against the third, this version follows the two.

What to watch. The rebuild's text edition and script were not in its folder, so its next-year earnings were taken as published.

Sources: the three source plans as published.

Evidence explains most of the fall from the earlier value.

Seven steps take Comvest's value from $14.86M in the 17 November plan to $6.73M. The two largest are a yield with no signed floor and the removal of cash at closing. Three steps take the independent plan's $5.52M up to the same figure.

What holds. Each step replaces an assumption with a record or with the more conservative end of the evidence.

What to watch. The steps are order-dependent, so each amount would differ if the order changed.

Sources: the published outputs of the 19 November rebuild.

Seven additions appear in none of the source plans.

This version adds a funding ladder, the existing credit line as a possible funding document, money owed to the company kept by the seller, a second reserve on the core-of-six plan, a loan sale as a decision-day outcome, retention tied to events, and the re-cut mandate.

What holds. Six of the seven are in the plan itself and need no private part to stand.

What to watch. The second reserve rests on CreditSwan's own operating review, which is why the plan asks the officer and the banker to test it.

Sources: Annex Z of the private master.

Commercial Diligence & Diagnostics

The only platform putting commercial diligence behind every number.

Deal Diligence

One committee-ready answer on a consumer deal, with the evidence attached. The pack verifies revenue and cost against source records, reconciled to the bank; tests customers, channels, brand, supply chain and the competitive set; and delivers the recommendation, the findings and the source trail, with covenants set to the evidence, at a three-day median from data access. The diligence does not stop at the pack. Dynamic Diagnostics keeps the same evidence live: a go / no-go read in days, before anyone commits to a process, and a weekly board of 20+ monitors after close, with a diagnosis for every breach.

For private lenders underwriting a borrower, PE sponsors before the LOI, and CEOs on their own business.

Dynamic Diagnostics keeps the diligence evidence live: what moved this week, why, and what to do about it

The same source systems the pack was built from, read again every week. Each series is tested against its threshold, and anything that breaches gets a written diagnosis and a next step. You hear about drift in week three, instead of at the quarterly certificate.

20+ monitors on every board across revenue, pricing, inventory, acquisition, retention, concentration and covenant headroom, each with a registered threshold and read every week

For lenders and sponsorsCovenant headroom and early warning on every portfolio company, read from the same systems the underwriting used, with a diagnosis attached and a named owner before anything changes.
For CEOsThe same board on your own business. What moved this week, why, and what to change, before your lender or your board asks the question.

How it is built

Raw exports and live APIs in, deterministic computation in the middle, lineage on every number out. AI does the compiling; credit analysts own every judgment.
